title: The Sasanian Empire: Rome's Eternal Rival

cards.b:
For four centuries, from about 224 to 651 CE, Rome and Persia were the two great powers of the west. They fought over Armenia, Mesopotamia and the trade routes between them.

The Sasanian Empire is less famous than Rome, but its story shows how a state can rise, fight a superpower, and then fall to a new faith and a new army.

Ardashir came from Persis, the homeland of the old Persian kings. Around 224 CE he defeated the last Parthian king and took over the Iranian plateau. He claimed descent from a priest called Sasan.

He built his capital at Ctesiphon, on the Tigris near modern Baghdad. Ardashir tied kingship to the religion of Zoroaster, and a priest named Kartir carved long texts praising the faith on rock walls.

In 260 CE Shapur I, Ardashir's son, defeated the Roman army at Edessa and captured the emperor Valerian. This was an enormous humiliation for Rome, the first time a reigning emperor was taken prisoner.

A rock relief at Naqsh-e Rustam shows Shapur on horseback, with Valerian kneeling before him. Persian kings used art like this to show their power to everyone who passed by.

Khosrow I Anushirvan (ruled 531–579)

Khosrow reformed taxes, the army and the land survey. Later Persian writers remembered him as the model of a just king. He made peace with Justinian in 562, a treaty known as the Fifty Years' Peace.

The peace was meant to last half a century. It broke down after about ten years, which tells you how fragile these deals were.
The empire lasted about four hundred years. Its last king died in exile in the east, while Arab armies took the western heartland.

cards.h: The trade of the Persian Gulf
cards.b:
The Sasanians controlled the Persian Gulf and much of the sea route to India and China. Persian merchants sold silk, spices and horses. Sogdian traders from Central Asia worked closely with them.

Ports on the Gulf coast were busy. Ships carried goods between Iraq, Iran and the Indian coast, so the empire earned a lot from tolls and taxes on trade.

cards.h: Were Rome and Persia always at war?
cards.b:
Many textbooks show Rome and Persia as eternal enemies. The image of two giants fighting for centuries is easy to remember.

Historians argue this is too simple. There were long periods of diplomacy, gift-giving and trade. The wars were mostly about buffer kingdoms like Armenia, and both sides often accepted peace when it suited them.

Khosrow II, a grandson of Khosrow I, won huge gains in the early 600s. Persian armies took Jerusalem in 614 and carried off the relic of the True Cross.

The emperor Heraclius struck back, invaded Persia and defeated its army near Nineveh in 627. Khosrow II was overthrown and killed in 628. Both empires were badly drained by the long war.

cards.h: A new power from the desert
cards.b:
After 632 the Arab armies of the new Islamic state moved fast. They defeated the exhausted Sasanian forces at Qadisiyya and took Ctesiphon. The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed in 651 at Merv while on the run.

Historians still debate how easily the Arabs conquered the empire. Some say the Sasanian state was already weakened by civil wars and tax revolts. Others stress the speed of the Arab advance.

The brick vault of the Taq Kasra at Ctesiphon is one of the great surviving arches of the ancient world. Its ruins still stand beside the Tigris.

Later Persian writers, including Ferdowsi in the Shahnameh (around 1010), kept Sasanian royal stories alive. Iranian national memory still draws on this era more than on the centuries that followed.

Khosrow I's court welcomed ideas from India. Indian animal fables were translated into Middle Persian as Kalila wa Dimna. The game of chaturanga also reached Persia, where it became shatranj, the ancestor of chess.

Persian and Indian merchants shared the same sea. Persian ships traded with the ports of western India, and the cultural exchange ran both ways.

Five things to remember
  1. The Sasanian Empire ruled Iran and Mesopotamia from 224 to 651 CE.
  2. Shapur I captured the Roman emperor Valerian in 260 CE.
  3. Khosrow I made the Fifty Years' Peace with Justinian in 562.
  4. Zoroastrianism was closely tied to the state.
  5. The Arab conquests ended the dynasty in the 650s.
Think about it
  • Why did long wars with Rome leave both empires weaker?
  • How did trade across the Gulf make Persia rich?
